subtopic_detail: sequencing blockade before surgery in a patient with episodic hypertension whose beta blocker was started first
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man referred with hypertension resistant to three agents. He describes episodes two or three times a week lasting about 20 minutes in which he sweats through his shirt, his heart pounds and he develops a severe throbbing headache, and he says he feels a sense of doom during them.

His general practitioner started metoprolol 50 mg twice daily nine days ago and he reports that since then the episodes have felt worse, with higher readings on his home monitor. His plasma free metanephrines are four times the upper reference limit on two separate occasions, and computed tomography shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units. Surgery has been discussed with the endocrine surgeons and he has no chest pain, no cardiac failure and a normal echocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 178/104, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and diaphoretic during an episode observed in clinic, no thyroid enlargement, no abdominal bruit, no neurocutaneous stigmata
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines four times the upper reference limit on two occasions, potassium and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue the metoprolol, add phenoxybenzamine, and proceed to surgery once the blood pressure settles
options.rationale: Adding alpha blockade does address the deficiency but leaving the beta blocker running through the interim continues the unopposed alpha stimulation that has already worsened his episodes. The sequence is what the question tests, and correcting it means stopping the beta blocker rather than layering over it. (Source: Endocrine Society: Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)

options.text: Continue the metoprolol, add amlodipine, and proceed to adrenalectomy within the next week
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are used as adjuncts where alpha blockade alone is insufficient or poorly tolerated, but they do not substitute for it, and operating within a week gives insufficient time for the volume re-expansion that alpha blockade allows. Inadequate preparation is the main driver of intraoperative hypertensive crisis and postoperative hypotension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the metoprolol, arrange metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy, and defer any blockade until it returns
options.rationale: Functional imaging has a role in assessing for metastatic or multifocal disease but does not change the need for preoperative blockade, and deferring treatment leaves him exposed to further paroxysms. Biochemical confirmation with a corresponding adrenal mass has already established the diagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society: Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)

options.text: Cease the metoprolol, arrange adrenal vein sampling, and commence spironolactone while awaiting results
options.rationale: Adrenal vein sampling and mineralocorticoid antagonism belong to the workup of primary aldosteronism, which is the other common cause of resistant hypertension with an adrenal lesion, but his potassium is normal and his catecholamine metabolites are four times the upper limit. The near pair distinction is which hormone the mass is producing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the metoprolol, commence phenoxybenzamine, and add a beta blocker later once blockade is established
options.rationale: Beta blockade given before alpha blockade removes beta 2 mediated vasodilatation while leaving alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which is why his episodes worsened after metoprolol was started, and it can precipitate hypertensive crisis or pulmonary oedema. Alpha blockade is established first over 10 to 14 days with liberal salt and fluid intake, and a beta blocker is added afterwards for reflex tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla, with paraganglioma the extra-adrenal equivalent, and it is worth pursuing in resistant hypertension, paroxysmal symptoms, an adrenal incidentaloma, or a relevant family syndrome such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, von Hippel-Lindau disease or the succinate dehydrogenase related syndromes. Plasma free metanephrines or 24 hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are the diagnostic tests of choice because the tumour metabolises catecholamines continuously while releasing them episodically. Unenhanced attenuation above 10 Hounsfield units excludes a lipid rich adenoma and is consistent with this diagnosis in the right biochemical context. Preoperative preparation is the part most often mishandled: alpha blockade first for 10 to 14 days with deliberate salt loading to re-expand a chronically constricted intravascular volume, then a beta blocker for reflex tachycardia only after that. Because a large proportion carry a germline mutation, genetic testing is now offered to essentially all patients regardless of family history.
key_points: Never start a beta blocker before alpha blockade, since unopposed alpha stimulation can precipitate crisis.
Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines are the diagnostic tests of choice.
Unenhanced attenuation above 10 Hounsfield units argues against a lipid rich adenoma.
Alpha blockade runs for 10 to 14 days with liberal salt and fluid to restore intravascular volume.
Offer germline genetic testing to essentially all patients, as a large minority carry a mutation.
explanation.pearls: Postoperative hypotension is expected once the tumour is removed, because the chronically alpha blocked and suddenly catecholamine deplete circulation is profoundly vasodilated, and it is treated with fluid rather than read as bleeding, which is why salt loading before surgery matters as much as the blockade itself.

subtopic_detail: separating two severe cutaneous adverse reactions when the rash appeared six weeks after an anticonvulsant was started
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 36-year-old woman with a widespread rash and fever. She started lamotrigine six weeks ago for bipolar disorder and the dose was escalated more quickly than the recommended schedule.

The rash began on her trunk four days ago and has spread to her limbs and face, and she says her face feels tight and swollen. There is no blistering anywhere, no skin pain and no ulceration of her mouth, eyes or genitals, and Nikolsky sign is negative. Her white cell count is 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with eosinophils of 1.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5) and atypical lymphocytes reported on the film. Her alanine aminotransferase is 384 U/L (less than 35) with a bilirubin of 24 micromol/L (less than 20), her creatinine is 118 micromol/L (45 to 90), and her thyroid function is within normal limits today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk, limbs and face with facial oedema; no blistering, no mucosal ulceration, Nikolsky sign negative; cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), eosinophils 1.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 384 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45 to 90)
data_table.Medication: Lamotrigine commenced 6 weeks ago with faster than recommended dose escalation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence systemic corticosteroid with monitoring of liver and renal function
options.rationale: Facial oedema, a morbilliform eruption, fever, eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and hepatic and renal involvement six weeks after starting an aromatic anticonvulsant is drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, which is treated by immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug and systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper. Organ involvement is what distinguishes it from a simple drug rash and is what mandates systemic treatment and prolonged monitoring. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and transfer to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which is the important near pair since lamotrigine causes both, but those conditions feature skin pain, blistering, mucosal ulceration and a positive Nikolsky sign. All four of those are explicitly absent and her eosinophilia with organ involvement points elsewhere. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Continue lamotrigine with oral antihistamine and topical corticosteroid for a simple drug eruption
options.rationale: A benign morbilliform drug eruption is managed this way, but it does not produce fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, transaminitis or renal impairment. Continuing the culprit drug through a systemic reaction risks progression to fulminant hepatitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence intravenous immunoglobulin as the primary treatment
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been used in toxic epidermal necrolysis with debated benefit and is not the established treatment for this reaction, where corticosteroid is the mainstay. Choosing it here applies the therapy of the near pair diagnosis rather than of the one she has. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start broad spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis with a reactive rash
options.rationale: Fever with a raised white cell count reasonably raises sepsis, and it is often treated empirically before the diagnosis is clear, but eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes is not a septic pattern and there is no source. Antibiotics also add further potential culprit drugs to a patient already reacting to one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a delayed T cell mediated hypersensitivity that characteristically begins two to eight weeks after the culprit drug is started, a latency far longer than that of a simple drug rash and a major reason the drug is not suspected. The commonest culprits are aromatic anticonvulsants including carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine, along with allopurinol, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline. Its defining features are fever, a widespread eruption with facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver but also the kidney, lung or heart. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses occurs during the reaction and is associated with relapse. Mortality is around 5 to 10 per cent, mostly from hepatic failure, and late autoimmune sequelae including thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes can appear months after apparent recovery, so follow up thyroid function and glucose testing is part of the discharge plan.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks separates this reaction from a simple morbilliform drug eruption.
Facial oedema, eosinophilia and organ involvement are the defining features.
Absent mucosal involvement, blistering and skin pain argue against Stevens Johnson syndrome.
Treatment is immediate drug withdrawal plus systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over weeks.
Arrange follow up thyroid function and glucose testing for late autoimmune sequelae.
explanation.pearls: Corticosteroid is tapered over six to twelve weeks rather than days, because a rapid wean commonly triggers a flare with recurrent fever and transaminitis, often coinciding with herpesvirus reactivation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

subtopic_detail: interpreting pleural fluid biochemistry that meets exudative criteria in a patient already treated with diuretics for heart failure
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman admitted four days ago with breathlessness and bilateral leg swelling. She has known heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30 per cent and has received intravenous furosemide 40 mg twice daily since admission, losing 5 kg.

Her breathlessness has improved but a right pleural effusion persists and you perform a diagnostic aspiration. The fluid is straw coloured and clear. Pleural protein is 32 g/L against a serum protein of 62 g/L, and pleural lactate dehydrogenase is 168 U/L against a serum value of 290 U/L with an upper reference limit of 250 U/L. The pleural glucose is 5.4 mmol/L, the pH is 7.42, and cytology and culture are pending. Her serum albumin is 33 g/L (35 to 50), she is afebrile, has no chest pain, and her C reactive protein is 4 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 in atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion at the right base with reduced breath sounds, jugular venous pressure 3 cm, ankle oedema reduced from admission
data_table.Pleural fluid: Straw coloured and clear; protein 32 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 168 U/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, pH 7.42, cytology and culture pending
data_table.Serum: Protein 62 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 290 U/L with upper reference limit 250 U/L, albumin 33 g/L (35 to 50), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: How would you interpret and act on these results?

options.text: Withhold further diuretic and repeat the pleural aspiration in 48 hours for a clearer result
options.rationale: Stopping treatment that is working in order to improve the interpretability of a test inverts the priority and risks decompensation. The albumin gradient resolves the ambiguity without any change to her treatment or a second procedure. (Source: BTS: Pleural Disease Guideline)

options.text: Calculate the serum to pleural albumin gradient, as diuresis can make a transudate appear exudative
options.rationale: Her pleural protein ratio of 0.52 meets exudative criteria, but diuresis concentrates protein and lactate dehydrogenase in a transudate and produces exactly this false exudate in roughly a quarter of diuresed heart failure effusions. A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L reclassifies the fluid as a transudate and prevents an unnecessary cascade of investigation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

options.text: Refer for thoracoscopic pleural biopsy, since the fluid meets exudative criteria on protein ratio
options.rationale: Applying the criteria mechanically without accounting for diuresis is the specific trap here, and thoracoscopy is an invasive step for an effusion with a straightforward cardiac explanation. Biopsy is warranted for an undiagnosed exudate after less invasive testing has failed. (Source: BTS: Pleural Disease Guideline)

options.text: Insert an intercostal catheter to drain the effusion completely and prevent re-accumulation
options.rationale: Chest drainage is indicated for empyema, a complicated parapneumonic effusion, or a large symptomatic effusion causing respiratory compromise, and her pH of 7.42 with a normal glucose and C reactive protein excludes infection. Her breathlessness is improving with medical therapy. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

options.text: Start empirical antibiotics for a parapneumonic effusion while awaiting the culture result
options.rationale: An infected effusion shows a pH below 7.2, a low glucose, a high lactate dehydrogenase and usually fever with a raised C reactive protein, and none of these is present. Treating empirically would expose her to antibiotic harm with no plausible indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as an exudate if the pleural to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, the pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio exceeds 0.6, or the pleural lactate dehydrogenase exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of the serum reference range. The criteria are deliberately sensitive for exudates and therefore misclassify a proportion of transudates, with diuresed heart failure the classic example because removing water concentrates the solutes left behind. When the clinical picture strongly suggests a transudate but the biochemistry says exudate, the serum to pleural albumin gradient resolves the conflict, with a value above 12 g/L indicating a transudate; the serum to pleural protein gradient above 31 g/L performs similarly. Recognising this saves patients from computed tomography, thoracoscopy and biopsy for an effusion that will resolve with treatment of the heart failure. A genuinely undiagnosed exudate, by contrast, warrants cytology, contrast enhanced imaging and tissue sampling, since malignancy and tuberculosis are the principal concerns.
key_points: Light's criteria are sensitive for exudates and misclassify some transudates, especially after diuresis.
A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L indicates a transudate despite exudative criteria.
Pleural pH below 7.2 with low glucose indicates a complicated parapneumonic effusion needing drainage.
Send protein, lactate dehydrogenase, glucose, pH, cytology and culture on every diagnostic aspirate.
Paired serum protein and lactate dehydrogenase must be taken at the same time as the pleural sample.
explanation.pearls: Pleural fluid pH must be measured on a blood gas analyser from a heparinised syringe kept anaerobic, because air exposure raises the pH and lidocaine contamination lowers it, and a falsely normal pH is what allows a complicated parapneumonic effusion to go undrained.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

subtopic_detail: distinguishing two neuromuscular junction disorders when strength improves rather than fatigues on repeated effort
stem:
You are the neurology registrar assessing a 63-year-old man with six months of difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing the stairs at home. He has smoked 40 cigarettes a day for 45 years.

He describes a dry mouth that he attributes to his blood pressure tablets and says he has become constipated. His eyelids are not droopy and he has no double vision, no difficulty chewing and no change to his voice or swallowing. On examination his hip flexors and shoulder abductors are graded 4 out of 5, and his knee and ankle reflexes are absent at rest. After he performs 15 seconds of maximal quadriceps contraction, you re-test the knee reflex and it is present, and his hip flexion strength is briefly graded 5 out of 5. His chest radiograph is reported as showing a right hilar fullness of uncertain significance.

data_table.Examination: Proximal limb weakness graded 4 out of 5 at hip flexors and shoulder abductors, areflexia at rest with reflexes returning after sustained contraction, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, no bulbar weakness, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase, thyroid function, electrolytes and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows right hilar fullness of uncertain significance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine to assess for a compressive myelopathy
options.rationale: Cord compression can cause leg weakness but produces increased tone, brisk reflexes below the level, extensor plantars and a sensory level, which is the opposite of his areflexic examination. Nothing in his presentation localises to the cord. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Nerve conduction studies looking for a demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy
options.rationale: Electrophysiology is genuinely central to this diagnosis, but the study required is repetitive nerve stimulation showing an incremental response at high frequency rather than a search for demyelination, and he has no sensory symptoms or signs. Framing the request as a polyneuropathy study risks the wrong protocol being performed. (Source: Brain Foundation Australia: Neuromuscular Disorders)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest with voltage gated calcium channel antibody testing
options.rationale: Post-exercise facilitation of reflexes and strength, areflexia at rest, proximal weakness and autonomic features such as dry mouth and constipation describe Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is paraneoplastic in around half of cases and associated overwhelmingly with small cell lung cancer in a heavy smoker. Finding the tumour is at least as urgent as confirming the antibody, because the neurological syndrome commonly precedes radiological diagnosis by months. (Source: Brain Foundation Australia: Neuromuscular Disorders)

options.text: Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing with computed tomography of the mediastinum for thymoma
options.rationale: This is the workup for myasthenia gravis, the near pair, but that condition fatigues with repeated effort rather than facilitating, preserves reflexes, and characteristically involves ocular and bulbar muscles which he explicitly lacks. Thymoma is its tumour association, whereas small cell lung cancer is the association here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with immunohistochemistry for an inflammatory myopathy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy is a reasonable thought given proximal weakness in an older adult, but it does not produce areflexia, autonomic dysfunction or post-exercise facilitation, and his creatine kinase is normal. Biopsy would delay the search for an underlying malignancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from antibodies against presynaptic voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantity of acetylcholine released with each nerve impulse, and roughly half of cases are paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer the dominant association. The clinical signature is the mirror image of myasthenia gravis: proximal lower limb weakness rather than ocular and bulbar involvement, depressed or absent reflexes rather than preserved ones, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and erectile dysfunction, and facilitation rather than fatigue with sustained effort. Repeated stimulation mobilises calcium in the presynaptic terminal and transiently improves transmission, which is why a reflex can be elicited only after exercise. Electrophysiology shows a low compound muscle action potential amplitude at rest with a marked increment after brief maximal exercise or high frequency repetitive stimulation. Treatment addresses the tumour where one is found, with amifampridine as symptomatic therapy and immunotherapy for those with persisting disability, and a negative initial cancer screen is repeated at intervals over the following two years.
key_points: Proximal weakness with areflexia and autonomic features distinguishes it from myasthenia gravis.
Facilitation after brief maximal exercise is the bedside sign; myasthenia fatigues instead.
Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, overwhelmingly with small cell lung cancer.
Repetitive nerve stimulation at high frequency shows an incremental response.
Repeat cancer screening over two years if the initial search is negative.
explanation.pearls: Amifampridine blocks presynaptic potassium channels, prolonging the action potential and increasing calcium entry so that more acetylcholine is released, and it is the symptomatic treatment of choice while the underlying tumour is being sought and treated.

subtopic_detail: recognising when pain and systemic toxicity outrun the visible skin findings in a limb infection
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who scraped his left shin on a trailer hitch three days ago. He was started on oral cefalexin by his general practitioner yesterday.

He is asking repeatedly for more analgesia and has already had oxycodone 10 mg and paracetamol without relief, describing the pain as far worse than the appearance suggests. The visible erythema extends about 10 cm around the abrasion with mild warmth and no fluctuance, and the marked border from yesterday has advanced 6 cm overnight. On palpation the calf feels firm and woody well beyond the area of redness, and he cannot tolerate light touch over that area. His white cell count is 22.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 164 micromol/L (60 to 110), C reactive protein 312 mg/L (less than 5), glucose 16.8 mmol/L and lactate 4.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, blood pressure 96/54, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythema 10 cm around the abrasion with woody induration extending well beyond it, exquisite tenderness out of proportion to appearance, no crepitus, no bullae, advancing 6 cm in 12 hours
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 164 micromol/L (60 to 110), C reactive protein 312 mg/L (less than 5), glucose 16.8 mmol/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2)
data_table.Treatment so far: Oral cefalexin since yesterday, oxycodone 10 mg and paracetamol without relief

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before surgical referral
options.rationale: Imaging can support the diagnosis by showing fascial oedema but is neither sensitive nor specific enough to exclude it, and arranging a scan in an unstable patient delays the only intervention that changes outcome. A normal scan would not be allowed to overrule the clinical picture, which means the scan cannot change management. (Source: Surgical Infection Society: Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Surgical Infection Society: Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Calculate a laboratory risk indicator score and refer to surgery only if the score exceeds the threshold
options.rationale: The laboratory risk indicator was derived to raise suspicion rather than to exclude the diagnosis, and it misses a meaningful proportion of cases, so a low score in a patient who looks like this must not reassure. Using a score as a gate for referral inverts its intended purpose. (Source: Surgical Infection Society: Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Surgical Infection Society: Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin with an insulin infusion and reassess the limb in six hours
options.rationale: Glycaemic control and cover for resistant organisms are both reasonable components of care, and his glucose does need treating, but neither addresses the necrotic tissue that antibiotics cannot penetrate because it has no blood supply. A six hour reassessment repeats the delay that drives mortality in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for exploration alongside resuscitation and broad spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion to the visible findings, woody induration beyond the erythema, rapid progression despite antibiotics, and systemic toxicity with hyponatraemia, renal impairment and a high lactate together indicate a necrotising soft tissue infection, in which survival depends on early surgical debridement. Antibiotics and resuscitation run in parallel but cannot substitute for the operation, and the diagnosis is made surgically rather than radiologically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Surgical Infection Society: Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin with limb elevation and review the margins in the morning
options.rationale: This is the correct pathway for cellulitis that has failed oral therapy, and it is exactly what the visible erythema invites, but it accepts a twelve hour delay in a disease where mortality rises with every hour to theatre. His pain, induration beyond the erythema and organ dysfunction all place him outside simple cellulitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection spreads along fascial planes, thrombosing the perforating vessels that supply the overlying skin, which is why the skin can look deceptively unremarkable while the tissue beneath is already dead and why systemic antibiotics reach the affected tissue poorly. The features that should override a reassuring appearance are pain disproportionate to the findings, induration extending beyond the visible erythema, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, and failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics. Later signs including bullae, skin necrosis, crepitus and anaesthesia over the affected skin are useful when present but their absence excludes nothing, and waiting for them costs time. Risk factors include diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, obesity and recent trauma or surgery. Management is immediate surgical exploration and debridement with repeated returns to theatre, broad spectrum antibiotics covering Gram positive, Gram negative and anaerobic organisms with an antitoxin agent such as clindamycin or lincomycin, and intensive care support.
key_points: Pain out of proportion to visible findings is the earliest and most useful warning sign.
Induration extending beyond the erythema indicates deep fascial involvement.
The diagnosis is surgical; imaging and scoring tools cannot exclude it.
Add clindamycin or lincomycin to suppress toxin production by streptococci and staphylococci.
Repeat debridement within 24 hours is planned rather than reactive.
explanation.pearls: Hyponatraemia with a sodium below 135 mmol/L in a patient with an apparent cellulitis is one of the most useful early laboratory discriminators for a necrotising infection and should trigger surgical review rather than a fluid prescription.

sources.label: Surgical Infection Society: Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection

subtopic_detail: interpreting a palpable purpuric rash with neuropathy and a very low complement component in a patient with abnormal liver enzymes
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 56-year-old woman with a six month history of a recurrent rash on both lower legs, aching in her hands and knees, and numbness in her feet.

The rash consists of raised purple spots that she can feel with her fingertips, comes in crops lasting about a week, and is worse after a day standing at work. She has burning numbness to mid shin bilaterally with reduced pinprick sensation and absent ankle reflexes. She had a blood transfusion after a road accident in 1988 and has never been tested for bloodborne viruses. Her alanine aminotransferase is 86 U/L (less than 35), her rheumatoid factor is strongly positive, her C4 is 0.02 g/L (0.15 to 0.55) with a C3 of 0.92 g/L (0.79 to 1.52), and her urinalysis shows blood and protein with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts on microscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, blood pressure 148/88, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over both lower legs, reduced pinprick to mid shin bilaterally with absent ankle reflexes, no synovitis, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 86 U/L (less than 35), rheumatoid factor strongly positive, C4 0.02 g/L (0.15 to 0.55), C3 0.92 g/L (0.79 to 1.52), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45 to 90)
data_table.Urinalysis: Blood and protein on dipstick with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts on microscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing with proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase specificities
options.rationale: These antibodies define the small vessel vasculitides that also cause purpura and glomerulonephritis, which makes this a genuine competing test, but those conditions are characteristically complement normal because they are pauci-immune. A C4 of 0.02 g/L points firmly to an immune complex process instead. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Vasculitis)

options.text: Anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing with radiographs of both hands and feet
options.rationale: A strongly positive rheumatoid factor with joint pain reasonably raises rheumatoid arthritis, and that is the trap this result sets, but she has no synovitis and rheumatoid arthritis does not cause palpable purpura with an active urinary sediment. Rheumatoid factor here reflects the cryoglobulin's own immunoglobulin M activity rather than rheumatoid disease. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Vasculitis)

options.text: Antinuclear antibody with double stranded DNA antibody testing for systemic lupus erythematosus
options.rationale: Lupus is an immune complex disease that does consume complement and can cause purpura, neuropathy and nephritis, but it characteristically lowers both C3 and C4 together rather than producing an isolated profound C4 reduction. The selective pattern is the discriminator between the two. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Vasculitis)

options.text: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains for a plasma cell disorder
options.rationale: A paraprotein can produce a type 1 cryoglobulin and a lymphoproliferative disorder is a recognised cause, so this belongs in the workup later, but it would not explain her transaminitis and is a less likely driver than chronic viral infection given her transfusion history. Testing for the treatable infection comes first. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C Management)

options.text: Hepatitis C serology with confirmatory viral load and serum cryoglobulin testing
options.rationale: Palpable purpura, peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia and glomerulonephritis with a disproportionately low C4 against a near normal C3 and a strongly positive rheumatoid factor is the classic serological pattern of mixed cryoglobulinaemia, which in the great majority of cases is driven by chronic hepatitis C. A transfusion in 1988 predates routine donor screening in Australia, which makes that the exposure to pursue. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C Management)

explanation.summary: Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that precipitate at temperatures below normal body temperature and redissolve on warming, and the mixed types containing both immunoglobulin M with rheumatoid factor activity and polyclonal immunoglobulin G form immune complexes that deposit in small vessels. Chronic hepatitis C accounts for the large majority of mixed cryoglobulinaemia, with the remainder associated with lymphoproliferative disease and connective tissue disorders. The clinical syndrome comprises palpable purpura on dependent areas, arthralgia, peripheral neuropathy and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, and the serological signature is a strongly positive rheumatoid factor with a profoundly low C4 and a relatively preserved C3. Sampling matters technically: the specimen must be collected and transported at 37 degrees Celsius, because a sample allowed to cool before separation gives a false negative. Treatment is directed at the cause, and direct acting antiviral therapy curing hepatitis C resolves the vasculitis in most patients, with rituximab and plasma exchange reserved for severe organ threatening disease.
key_points: A profoundly low C4 with a near normal C3 is the signature complement pattern.
Rheumatoid factor positivity reflects the cryoglobulin itself, not rheumatoid arthritis.
Chronic hepatitis C underlies the majority of mixed cryoglobulinaemia cases.
The clinical tetrad is purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy and glomerulonephritis.
Treat the underlying cause; direct acting antivirals resolve most hepatitis C associated disease.
explanation.pearls: A cryoglobulin sample must be collected into a pre-warmed tube and kept at 37 degrees Celsius until the serum is separated, because allowing it to cool in transit precipitates the cryoglobulin into the clot and produces a false negative that sends the workup in the wrong direction.
